\section[guadagnare]{guadagnare — to earn; to gain}

\label{lesson:IT-C398-guadagnare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the quote, then the Italian for good value.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: guadagnare}
\textbf{guadagnare} — \textquotedblleft{}to earn; to gain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se lavori il sabato, guadagni di più.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If you work on Saturdays, you earn more.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Guadagnarsi da vivere} — to earn a living. \emph{Guadagnare tempo} — to gain time.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{guadagnare} comes from a Germanic verb: EtymDB traces it through Vulgar Latin \emph{wadanio} \textquotedblleft{}to pursue, to win; to graze\textquotedblright{} to Proto-Germanic \emph{waiþanjaną} (EtymDB). Italian turned the Germanic \emph{w-} into \emph{gu-}, as in \emph{guerra}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{guadagnare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{guadagnare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the quote, then the Italian for good value, then say \emph{guadagnare} again
\end{itemize}

\section[il guadagno]{il guadagno — the earnings, the gain}

\label{lesson:IT-C398-guadagno}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for good value, then the Italian for to earn.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il guadagno}
\textbf{il guadagno} — \textquotedblleft{}the earnings, the gain\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con il guadagno della vendita ho comprato una moto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{With the money from the sale I bought a motorbike.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{guadagnare}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{guadagno} is built on \emph{guadagnare} \textquotedblleft{}to earn\textquotedblright{}, from a Germanic verb that EtymDB traces through Vulgar Latin \emph{wadanio} \textquotedblleft{}to pursue, to win\textquotedblright{} to Proto-Germanic \emph{waiþanjaną} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[il profitto]{il profitto — the profit; the benefit}

\label{lesson:IT-C398-profitto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to earn, then the Italian for the earnings.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il profitto}
\textbf{il profitto} — \textquotedblleft{}the profit; the benefit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
L'azienda ha fatto un profitto di un milione.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The company made a profit of a million.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Trarre profitto da} — to benefit from. At school, \emph{il profitto} is progress.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{profitto} came from Old French \emph{profit} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{prōfectus} \textquotedblleft{}progress, gain, profit\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{prōficere} \textquotedblleft{}to make progress, to be useful\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{facere} \textquotedblleft{}to make\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la perdita]{la perdita — the loss; the leak}

\label{lesson:IT-C398-perdita}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the earnings, then the Italian for the profit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la perdita}
\textbf{la perdita} — \textquotedblleft{}the loss; the leak\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se vendi adesso, è una perdita.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If you sell now, it is a loss.}
\end{quote}

Stress on the first syllable: \emph{pèrdita}. A water leak is also \emph{una perdita}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{perdita} is built on \emph{perdere} \textquotedblleft{}to lose\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{perdere} \textquotedblleft{}to destroy, to lose\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{per-} and \emph{dare} \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{}: to give away for good.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[fallire]{fallire — to go bankrupt; to fail}

\label{lesson:IT-C398-fallire}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the profit, then the Italian for the loss.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fallire}
\textbf{fallire} — \textquotedblleft{}to go bankrupt; to fail\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se nessuno compra, il negozio fallisce.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If no one buys, the shop will go bust.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated with \emph{-isc-}: \emph{fallisce}. \emph{Fallire un esame} — to fail an exam.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fallire} is inherited from Vulgar Latin \emph{fallīre}, a form of Latin \emph{fallere} \textquotedblleft{}to deceive, to escape notice, to fail\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
